short: Four months that ended two thousand years of imperial rule in China.
full:
The Qing court's decision in 1911 to nationalise provincial railway lines and mortgage them to foreign banks provoked mass protest in Sichuan, and troops were moved from Hubei to suppress it. On 9 October a bomb exploded by accident in the revolutionaries' Hankou headquarters, exposing their membership lists. Rather than wait to be arrested, the New Army garrison at Wuchang mutinied the next day, 10 October, and seized the city, pressing a reluctant senior officer to lead them.

The rising spread by provincial declaration rather than by battle: fifteen provinces had renounced Qing authority within seven weeks. Delegates meeting at Nanjing proclaimed the Republic of China on 1 January 1912 with Sun Yat-sen as provisional president. The court's answer was to recall Yuan Shikai, the only man who commanded the modernised northern army, and he used the position to negotiate with both sides at once. On 12 February 1912 the empress dowager issued an abdication edict for the six-year-old Puyi, and the imperial system that began in 221 BCE ended.
